look_here_first: LOW, sprawling or mat-forming plant; leaves OPPOSITE, oval-to-triangular and shallowly toothed. Tiny YELLOW composite heads sit almost directly in the LEAF AXILS (where leaf meets stem). Confirm the Asteraceae head: short ray florets around yellow disc florets; inspect the green phyllaries beneath the head and, when mature, small awned cypselae. Do not identify by yellow flower color alone.

taxonomic_note: Calyptocarpus vialis Less. is the accepted name per Kew POWO. Synedrella vialis is an older homotypic name; do not confuse it with Synedrella nodiflora, a different species. Species is reported native to Texas by POWO; defer strict target-county nativity labels under project policy.

best_field_traits: Creeping/procumbent perennial; delicate branched shoots spread through thin turf or along path edges and can root at nodes.
Leaves in opposite pairs, often rotated 90 degrees at successive nodes (decussate); one simple blade per petiole.
Leaf blades usually ovate, broadly lanceolate or somewhat triangular (deltate), about 1–3 cm commonly, sometimes larger; shallow rounded teeth on margins; three prominent veins arise near the base.
Single small yellow COMPOSITE head about 4–8 mm across, nearly stalkless (subsessile), nestled where a leaf meets the stem.
Small ray florets are present but have short yellow limbs; inner yellow disc florets are separate tiny flowers, not a single disc.
Beneath a head inspect a few green overlapping phyllaries (typically about 4–6), not ordinary flower sepals.
In fruit, look for flattened dry one-seeded cypselae with two conspicuous barbed awns (small additional awns may occur).
morphology_keys.life_cycle: Perennial herb; can regrow from its established plant base and spreading branches. Flowering reported nearly year-round across its geographic range, but Central Texas flowering varies with rain, mowing and frost.
morphology_keys.growth_habit: Prostrate to decumbent (trailing or partly lifted), branched herb, roughly 4–27 cm high and stems to about 40 cm long in the UT Williamson County treatment; sometimes forms loose mats among turf. Look for roots at contacting nodes, not tall vertical stalks.
morphology_keys.stem: Slender cylindrical green or sometimes red-striped/purplish stems, hairy with short, mostly upward-pointing stiff hairs (strigose), branching at nodes. Shoot tips can rise despite generally creeping habit.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Opposite and decussate: leaves emerge in pairs from each node; successive pairs typically cross in orientation. Not alternate and not three leaflets.
morphology_keys.leaves: Simple, small, petiolate blades; ovate to deltate (triangular-ovate), sometimes broadly lanceolate; low crenate-serrate teeth, not smooth coin-shaped margins; short appressed hairs on both surfaces. Williamson County measured 6.5–54 mm long × less than 5–28 mm wide, with variation.
morphology_keys.leaf_venation: Often three principal veins arising near the leaf base plus pinnate secondary venation. Veins assist confirmation but overlap with other small herbs; do not identify from three basal veins alone.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Usually a solitary radiate CAPITULUM (flower head) at a leaf axil; heads very short-stalked or nearly stalkless (subsessile). A leafy branch may continue immediately beside the head, making the head seem part of a cluster.
morphology_keys.heads: Typically ~4–8 mm across. What looks like one tiny flower is a composite head of multiple separate yellow florets: short outer ray florets and central disc florets.
morphology_keys.phyllaries: Small overlapping green involucral bracts beneath the head, often 4–6; Williamson County describes a bell-shaped involucre ~5–6 mm long. These are crucial Asteraceae organs; not yet verified in existing gallery photos.
morphology_keys.flower: Yellow ray florets bear a short straplike corolla with lobes at the tip; central yellow disc florets are tubular and bisexual. Number and visibility vary; check with a hand lens rather than expecting a large showy daisy.
morphology_keys.fruit: Cypsela (dry one-seeded fruit, often called an achene), typically ~2–4 mm long; often flattened and sometimes somewhat angled, with usually two conspicuous spreading-to-ascending barbed awns of the pappus (smaller additional awns possible). Fruit angle is NOT invariably three-sided.
morphology_keys.habitat: Warm Central Texas lawns and lightly shaded turf margins, path edges, garden beds, roadsides and other disturbed ground; tolerates several soil types including clays and calcareous soils. Habitat is supporting, not an ID character.
morphology_keys.field_season: In Central Texas, look for leaves and spreading runners across much of the growing season, tiny heads during warm or moist spells; flowering may pause in dry or freezing weather. FNA reports flowering approximately year-round geographically; do not promise year-round local blooms.
morphology_keys.measurement_tip: Flower head ~4–8 mm across, far smaller than most conspicuous daisies. Carry a 1 mm-rule/hand lens for phyllaries and small awned fruit.
morphology_keys.key_cautions: Low stature plus yellow color is insufficient. Opposite leaves and short yellow rays are shared with other herbs; the almost stalkless axillary capitulum and reproductive microstructure are strongest checks. A 3-angled cypsela is possible but not universal.

confused_with: Synedrella nodiflora (introduced tropical comparison; not assumed locally frequent)
comparisons.key_distinctions: Frogfruit: tiny white/pink flowers crowded into a button/cylinder on a noticeable naked axillary stalk, rather than a yellow ray-and-disc composite head. Carolina ponyfoot: round or kidney-shaped, entire-margined ALTERNATE leaves on long petioles, and minute non-daisy flowers. False daisy (Eclipta): opposite but much narrower/larger leaves; many short WHITE ray florets in a larger head, often wetter habitats. Hairy wedelia: much larger yellow/orange flower heads on longer peduncles and taller, coarse, often woody-based stems. Synedrella nodiflora: a useful botanical comparison in introduced floras, more erect with clustered heads; local occurrence should be checked before making it a core Hays field target.

comparisons.caution: Do not treat all low mat-forming plants as close botanical relatives: Phyla is in Verbenaceae and Dichondra in Convolvulaceae; they are practical same-site comparisons. Eclipta and Wedelia share Asteraceae but differ in floral scale/structure.

ecological_notes.crew_encounters: Frequently encountered as a volunteer/groundcover in turf transitions, footpath edges, beds and partly shaded park ground. The crew should learn it as a recognizable existing plant before deciding whether any site-specific management is needed.
ecological_notes.mowing_and_weather: Low growth permits persistence in some mowed lawns, but repeated low mowing, drought and frost affect how many flowers are visible. Do not decide identity or remove it based only on sparse flowering.
ecological_notes.ecological_claims: Small composite flowers can offer floral resources, but no numerical local specialist-bee or Lepidoptera host totals have been verified for this card. Do not present speculative species-specific counts.
ecological_notes.native_range_note: Kew POWO recognizes a native range including Texas. Detailed target-county nativity verification remains outside this manual morphology pass.

family_genus_teaching.family: Asteraceae: a capitulum is a head of many tiny florets; green phyllaries form the involucre underneath; the dry one-seeded fruit is a cypsela.
family_genus_teaching.genus: Calyptocarpus: low opposite-leaved herbs with small yellow radiate heads; use the short-stalked axillary heads plus awned fruits to separate this taxon from unrelated creeping groundcovers.
family_genus_teaching.species: C. vialis: conspicuously low branching habit, mostly ovate-to-triangular short-toothed opposite leaves, ~4–8 mm heads at axils, overlapping green phyllaries and awned cypselae.
